explanations.explanation: Not quite, friend. Paul, the apostle writing this letter to Timothy, says that person is conceited and understands nothing. Nothing! There's no spot in there for "knows it all but says it badly." I think a lot of us would love that to be the case, but Paul's word is plain.

That's right, friend. Paul, the apostle writing this letter to Timothy, says this teacher is "…conceited and understands nothing." He doesn't say the man has the truth and just fumbles the delivery. Teaching against the sound words of our Lord Jesus Christ (1 Timothy 6:3) isn't a speaking problem. Paul says it's an understanding problem.

explanations.answer: Envy and strife and evil suspicions
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. Paul says envy, strife, abusive talk and evil suspicions come out of those controversies and disputes about words. That's a whole basket of trouble. Nobody walks away from a word fight with a trophy.

I'd love for that to be the harvest, friend. But Paul lists what really comes out of those disputes: envy, strife, abusive talk and evil suspicions. Patience, kindness and peace aren't on his list. Fighting over words is a bad way to grow them.

Those are good things, friend, but they aren't what Paul says comes out. He names envy, strife, abusive talk and evil suspicions. Remember, he already called this teacher conceited, and conceit and humility don't share a counter. Wisdom, humility and trust never make the list.

You got it, baker. Paul says these men regard godliness as a means of gain. In other words, they treat it like a way to get something. Hold onto that, because Paul is about to flip it on its head in the very next verse.

That sounds lovely, friend, but it's not what Paul says. He says these men regard godliness as a means of gain. Notice who he's talking about: men of depraved mind who are devoid of the truth. Peace isn't the word he uses for what they see in it.

A nap would be nice, friend, but Paul doesn't say that. He says these men regard godliness as a means of gain. They're looking at godliness and seeing what they can get out of it. Rest never comes up.
That's it, baker. Paul says, "For we brought nothing into the world, so we cannot carry anything out of it." Nothing in, nothing out. Not even a carry-on bag!

explanations.answer: Nothing in and a little out
explanations.explanation: You've got the first half, friend. We brought nothing into the world. But the second half is also nothing, because Paul says we cannot carry anything out of it. Not even a little. I checked the verse twice, and there's no room for a small bag.

explanations.answer: A little in and nothing out
explanations.explanation: The second half is right, friend. We cannot carry anything out of the world. But Paul starts earlier than that, and he says we brought nothing into the world. So it's nothing at both doors. Zero on the way in and zero on the way out.
Yes, friend. Paul says, "But if we have food and clothing, we will be content with these." Food and clothing, and that's the list. My apron counts, and I'm very content with it.

I see why you'd go there, friend. But Paul says food and clothing, not money. Money is where he heads next, and he has some careful things to say about it. For the contentment he's describing here, he stops at food and clothing.
That's a big ask, friend! Paul doesn't say land. He says, "But if we have food and clothing, we will be content with these." It's a short list, and no deed is on it.

That's right, friend. Paul says those who want to be rich fall into temptation. Notice he's talking about wanting to be rich, not the people who have a little in the cupboard. The wanting is where the falling starts.

That would be a nice landing, friend, but Paul says something else. Those who want to be rich fall into temptation. A fall doesn't usually end somewhere soft. Paul keeps going from there, and it doesn't get easier.
You'd think so, friend! But Paul says those who want to be rich fall into temptation. He doesn't say they land in abundance. The wanting itself is the trouble he's pointing at.

That's right, friend. Paul says those foolish and harmful desires "…plunge them into ruin and destruction." Plunge is a strong word, like a dive with no water at the bottom. I'm glad Paul tells us ahead of time.

Paul actually says it, friend. He says those many foolish and harmful desires "…plunge them into ruin and destruction." It's in the verse about those who want to be rich. So the statement is true. It's a heavy line.

Yes, baker. Paul says, "For the love of money is the root of all kinds of evil." It's the love of it, not the money sitting there. A quarter in a pocket isn't the trouble. Hearts holding on too tight is what Paul has his eye on.

I get the thought, friend, because having too little is hard. But Paul doesn't say that. He says it's the love of money that's the root of all kinds of evil. His target is what we love, not what we're missing.

Close to the register, friend, but not quite. Paul says it's the love of money that's the root of all kinds of evil. He isn't talking about how much goes out of the wallet. He's talking about what's going on in the heart.
That's right, friend. Paul says that by craving money, some have wandered away from the faith. It sounds quiet, like a wander and not a leap. I think that's what makes it so sneaky.
That would be a happy ending, friend, but Paul says the opposite. By craving money, some have wandered away from the faith. They didn't grow in it. They drifted off.

explanations.answer: They held on to it tightly
explanations.explanation: That's the opposite of what Paul says, friend. He says that by craving money, some have wandered away from the faith. The tight grip went on the money, and the faith got loose. Paul's picture is of people walking off.
You've got it, friend. Paul says that by craving money, some have "…pierced themselves with many sorrows." Themselves! That's a hard line to read. Better to catch it early.

You'd expect somebody else to hold the sharp end, friend. But Paul says some "…pierced themselves with many sorrows." He doesn't mention any enemies in the picture. It's a hard line, and I think it's meant to be.
Paul doesn't blame friends, friend. He says that by craving money, some "…pierced themselves with many sorrows." Nobody else is in the verse holding the point. I think this one hurts.
